I work the night shift at the front desk, so let me tell you exactly what happens here. Around eleven the ferry people start arriving, all of them tired, and half of them with a reservation I cannot find on the first try. Here is the part nobody believes. The guest who says could you check the name again, please, gets a room faster than the guest who makes a speech. It is not because I like him more. It is because I can actually listen. And if the room really is gone, I almost always have an alternative somewhere in the building: a smaller one, a higher one, a quieter one. But I offer it to the people who ask me a question, not to the people who bring me a complaint. So if your check-in goes wrong at midnight, use ten words instead of a hundred, and keep the receipt where you can find it.

My advice comes from one very bad night in Split. The ferry was two hours late, the evening shift had already gone home, and the man on duty told me there was no reservation under my name. I had paid in June. What saved me was not my temper. It was a photograph. I had the receipt on my phone, with the booking number on it, and I asked him one question: could you check that number for me, please. It took him forty seconds. The reservation was there, spelled with a different letter. So now I do three things before every trip. I save the receipt as a photograph, I write the booking number on paper as well, and I learn how to say would it be possible in the local language. Two of those three have never failed me.

First the ferry from Split arrived two hours late, and he reached the hotel close to midnight. Then the man at the front desk looked for his name on the screen and could not find the reservation anywhere. After that he opened the photograph of the receipt on his phone and asked whether the man could check the booking number instead. At that point the reservation appeared, spelled with one different letter, but the original room was no longer available. In the end they gave him an alternative on the top floor, smaller and much quieter, and he decided that the delay had been worth it.
